cards.title: Linear-time directed bottleneck paths and trees
cards.formal: Do the directed bottleneck path and rooted bottleneck spanning-tree problems admit comparison-based algorithms with expected running time \(O(n+m)\) on every input, always returning an exact optimum? The input has \(n\) vertices and \(m\) weighted directed edges. Randomization is allowed; deterministic linear time would also answer positively. The source writes \(O(m)\) after the usual removal or treatment of irrelevant vertices. The requested guarantee is total running time, including graph processing and output, with weights accessible only through comparisons.
cards.why: Determines the exact cost of fundamental directed min-max optimization when numerical information is available only by comparison. Removing the overhead would close a long-standing gap for sparse graphs; distinguishing the input model prevents an already-solved variant from being presented as open.
cards.status_note: Checked the original definitions, Theorem 3, both reductions, the word-RAM result and the exact Section 7 questions, plus the August 2026 v2 preprint including its counterexample and reduction statement. The main target permits always-correct randomization, matching the preceding expected-time theorem; the separate deterministic near-linear question is not silently substituted. Searches through 12 September 2026 found no resolution. The recent correction is a preprint and its proofs were not independently audited.

progress.text: Theorem 3 improves the comparison-based expected time to O(mβ(m,n)); Section 5 separately gives deterministic linear time when word-RAM operations on weights are allowed.

references.title: Bottleneck Paths and Trees and Deterministic Graphical Games
references.authors: Chechik, Shiri; Kaplan, Haim; Thorup, Mikkel; Zamir, Or; Zwick, Uri
references.locator: Unresolved-question passage on page 12; PDF page 12

cards.definitions:
In the bottleneck path problem (BP), the input is an explicit directed graph G=(V,E), a source s, a target t and a weight w(e) for every edge. Among all directed s-to-t paths P, output one minimizing max_{e∈P}w(e). Any optimal simple path is acceptable; ties require no prescribed choice. If t is unreachable, report that no path exists. When s=t the empty path is returned, with bottleneck conventionally −∞.

In the bottleneck spanning-tree problem (BST), the input is the same kind of directed weighted graph and a specified root s. Output an out-arborescence T spanning all vertices: s has indegree zero, every other vertex has indegree one in T, and there is a directed path in T from s to every vertex. Minimize max_{e∈T}w(e). If no such tree exists, report this. For a one-vertex graph, the empty tree has value −∞. This objective minimizes the single largest tree-edge weight, not the sum of weights. A tree minimizing that largest weight need not supply an individually optimal bottleneck path to every vertex.

Weights are arbitrary elements of a totally ordered set, such as arbitrary real numbers. They are opaque keys: they may be stored, copied and compared in constant time, but their digits, arithmetic values and integer ranks are not available for computation. Equal weights are allowed. The graph is given by adjacency lists with O(log(n+m+2))-bit vertex and edge indices; ordinary operations on these indices have unit cost. The algorithm is charged for all graph operations, comparisons, random sampling and writing its path or tree, not just the number of comparisons. There is no assumption that the weights are sorted, bounded integers, or machine words supporting bit operations.

The randomization convention is Las Vegas: on every fixed input the answer is exact, termination occurs with probability one, and the expected total work over the algorithm's internal random choices is at most C(n+m) for a universal constant C. This includes feasibility checks and output. A randomized algorithm with a small probability of an incorrect optimum would not meet this convention. For BP, isolated and unreachable vertices can be removed in O(n+m) work. A feasible nontrivial BST instance has m≥n−1. Thus O(n+m) makes the source's O(m) target meaningful also on degenerate explicit inputs without changing its substantive content.

The question asks for this guarantee for both tasks, but their expected-linear-time versions are equivalent through the reductions in Section 4 of the source. These reductions do not establish the corresponding deterministic equivalence: the BST-to-BP reduction uses randomness. The source's separate question about a deterministic O(mβ(m,n)) bound is not the target of this card. Neither all-pairs bottleneck paths nor finding every individual single-source bottleneck value is required.
cards.answer_criterion: Give always-correct comparison-based algorithms with expected O(n+m) total work for both directed tasks, or use the source reductions to derive both guarantees from one. Alternatively, rule out such algorithms, stating any assumptions used. An undirected algorithm, a word-RAM algorithm inspecting weight representations, a bound on comparisons alone, or a faster algorithm only for sufficiently dense graphs does not settle the unrestricted target. A deterministic lower bound alone does not rule out the permitted randomized algorithms.

cards.title: Uniform compressed word problem for graph groups
cards.formal: Is there a single deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given a finite simple graph \((A,I)\) and a straight-line program \(S\) over \(A^{\pm1}\), decides whether \(\operatorname{val}(S)=1\) in the graph group \(G(A,I)=\langle A\mid ab=ba\text{ for }(a,b)\in I\rangle\)? The time bound must be polynomial in the combined encoded size of the graph and the program, uniformly over all graphs. This is the polynomial-time branch of the source question; membership in NP is its separate, weaker intermediate target.
cards.why: Asks whether efficient algebraic computation survives when both a compressed group element and the commutation structure of its ambient group vary. It isolates a uniformity obstacle that remains after fixed-group algorithms and more restricted compressed representations have been handled.
cards.status_note: Read the conference definitions and Remark 10, the indexed primary author-manuscript Section 3.6, and the 2024 publisher full-text introduction. The old journal-manuscript PDF redirect prevented a local full download; journal dates were checked against publisher-deposited metadata. Searches through 12 September 2026 found no resolution of the uniform arbitrary-SLP question. The formal question explicitly selects P-membership and retains NP as a weaker branch, not an equivalent formulation.

upgraded_from.title: Uniform compressed word problem for graph groups

references.title: Knapsack in Graph Groups, HNN-Extensions and Amalgamated Products
references.locator: Unresolved-question passage on page 10; PDF page 10

cards.definitions:
A graph group, also called a right-angled Artin group, has one generator for every vertex in A. An edge specifies that its two generators commute. I is symmetric and has no loops. The displayed presentation imposes these commutation relations and the group axioms, with no additional relations such as a²=1. The alphabet A±1 contains each generator and a formal inverse. Products are identified under insertion or deletion of adjacent inverse pairs and interchange of adjacent commuting letters, including their inverses. The identity is the class of the empty word. For instance aba⁻¹b⁻¹ is the identity when a and b are joined by an edge; without that edge, it is nontrivial in the two-generator free group.

A straight-line program is an acyclic sequence of string assignments. In a convenient normal form, X_i is assigned an alphabet letter, the empty word, or a concatenation X_jX_k with j,k<i. A designated final variable produces val(S). Reusing a variable means reusing its whole generated string; it does not introduce a new unknown group element. General finite right-hand sides can be put in this form with polynomial overhead. The expanded string can have exponential length in the program size and is not given explicitly.

Vertices and variables have binary indices. The graph is given explicitly, for example by its vertex and edge lists, and every program instruction is listed explicitly. Let L be the total bit length of this representation. The requested bound is L^{O(1)} bit operations on a deterministic machine, with one exponent and one algorithm for the entire input family. It cannot hide an arbitrary dependence on |A| or the commutation graph in a supposedly fixed constant. Equivalent explicit encodings differing by polynomial factors give the same P-membership question. Ill-formed graphs or cyclic programs may be rejected in polynomial time.

For the weaker NP question, every identity instance would need a certificate of length polynomial in L verifiable deterministically in polynomial time; nonidentity instances must have no accepting certificate. The known coRP result instead gives a randomized polynomial-time identity test that always accepts identities and accepts any nonidentity with probability at most 1/3. This does not by itself put identity instances in NP. The target concerns an arbitrary compressed word, not merely a product u₁^{z₁}⋯u_t^{z_t} of explicitly written words with given binary integer exponents, and not the existence of unknown exponents.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove uniform deterministic polynomial-time decidability for arbitrary input commutation graphs and SLPs, or prove that no such algorithm exists, stating any complexity assumption used by a conditional obstruction. An NP upper bound is progress on the weaker branch and must not be reported as a positive answer to P-membership. A bound polynomial only for each fixed group, or an algorithm restricted to power words, does not settle this card.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
